blogs.title: The Perils of Confusing Expert Testimony: How Self-Contradiction Can Topple a Jury Verdict
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's reversal on the '134 patent, focusing on the court's strict application of the *substantial evidence* standard to expert witness credibility. The article will dissect Chief Judge Moore's reasoning regarding Dr. Jonathan Wells' contradictory testimony, specifically his shifting identification of 'signals of interest' versus 'interference generating signals.' It will explore the precedent set by *Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope Corp.* discussed in the opinion, offering practical guidance for litigators on how to manage expert witnesses to prevent self-inflicted JMOL reversals.

blogs.title: Seven Multiplications Matter: The Strict Literalism Required for Digital Signal Processing Claims
blogs.description: Focusing on the '775 patent, this post examines the Federal Circuit's refusal to allow functional equivalents or vague mappings when claim language specifies exact numerical steps (seven multiplications of three signals). The analysis will contrast the district court's acceptance of a 'mapping' theory against the appellate court's demand for concrete evidence that all seven specific mathematical operations were performed. Furthermore, it will address why the court rejected Finesse's argument that amending claims from 'two or three' to 'three' did not constitute a surrender of scope involving only two unique input signals, clarifying the nuances of prosecution history estoppel in algorithmic patents.

blogs.title: When Technical Complexity Meets Legal Certainty: Why Documentary Evidence Must Match Claim Language Exactly
blogs.description: This entry discusses the evidentiary gap exposed in *Finesse Wireless*, where Nokia's internal technical documents described modulus and complex conjugate operations rather than the literal multiplications required by the patent claims. The post will analyze how courts handle cases where accused technology performs similar functions but via mathematically distinct processes than those recited in the claims. It will serve as a warning to plaintiffs that relying on high-level summaries in technical documentation without explicitly linking them to every element of a claim—even in highly technical fields like PIM cancellation—creates fatal vulnerabilities at trial.
